Recordings from the changeover weekend sometimes carry a device's confused hour. A one-hour shift is the surgical repair when the offset is uniform.

Duration before: 4:24:36. Duration after the shift: 4:24:36. Speeds, distances, elevation — untouched. Only the stamps' reading on the clock changes, which is the definition of a pure time translation.
A stamp at 23:40 becomes 00:40 the next day after the shift — the date moves with the time, correctly, because the tool shifts instants, not clock-face text.

popular_table.note: GPX stamps are UTC (the Z suffix) by the format's convention. Shifting is the right repair only when the recording's offset from truth is a constant hour — a device that drifted gradually needs different medicine.

faq: The classic errors are one-hour errors: a timezone mis-set by one zone, a DST toggle missed. This tool implements that single, well-defined repair rather than a free-form editor — if your offset is different, the honest options are a text-level edit or a fuller tool.
What if my offset is 30 minutes (or 5:30)?

Some zones differ by half hours, and a device set to one of those needs a 30-minute correction this fixed shift does not perform. The file's stamps can be adjusted in a text editor with care — every <time> by the same amount.
Does it handle the date change at midnight?
Yes — shifting instants rolls dates forward correctly, including month and year boundaries, because the arithmetic is on timestamps, not on clock text.
The mirror error exists (a file stamped an hour ahead). Where the tool offers direction, choose it; the invariant guarantees — duration, geometry — hold in both directions.
The metadata <time> shifts with the trackpoints: a corrected file should be consistent in its header too, or the next tool to read it inherits the confusion.
Check the other clock: cameras drift and get set wrong independently. Align one known moment (a photo of the trailhead sign against the track's start) and compute the true offset.
